positions.position: The Resurrection's occurrence or rising, conceived as a single forceful, momentous event.
positions.reasons: Al-Dāmghānī glosses waqaʿa as arising or coming to pass and identifies the Occurrence as Resurrection. Al-Rāzī stresses one occurrence, all at once. Al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı trace waqʿa from a forceful fall to a great event or crisis, sometimes specifically war; al-Ālūsī identifies this instance as Resurrection.

question: What does the lām in li-waqʿatihā express?

positions.position: It marks the time when the Event occurs.
positions.reasons: Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī compare 89:24. Al-Ālūsī and al-Kashf take it temporally in the denial and self-encouragement readings. Ibn ʿĀshūr derives this temporal use from specification and compares 17:78, 65:1, and 7:143; he cites the Prophet's statement that prayer at its proper time is the best deed, without grading, and distinguishes 88:6. Bursawī gives this as one option.

positions.position: It gives the cause: the Event's overwhelming occurrence leaves no room for lying or false report.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī says its overwhelming occurrence stops lying or false denial, unlike denial before it. Bursawī gives a causal alternative in which nothing reported of the Event is false.

positions.position: It marks the object or relation of the lying: no one falsifies the Event in reporting it.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī explicitly contrasts this relational reading with the causal lām.

turns_on: Whether the lām locates the denial in time, gives the occurrence as its cause, or relates denial to the Event as its object.

question: How is kādhibatun grammatically formed and construed?

positions.position: It is an abstract or verbal noun for lying, denial, or falsehood, despite its participial shape.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Qushayrī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī compare ʿāqiba and ʿāfiya; some add nāzila. Al-Kisāʾī compares lāghiya in 88:11 and khāʾina; al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī cite qāʾiman for qiyāman and a woman's rhyme, and al-Qurṭubī adds ʿāʾidhan bi-llāh. Al-Burhān and al-Itqān state the general agent-or-object noun for action rule, the latter comparing al-maftūn and saying its bāʾ is not redundant. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Samīn give takdhīb and compare khāʾinat al-aʿyun. Al-Ālūsī notes a reservation: fāʿila is rare as a verbal noun. Al-Naḥḥās makes kādhibatun the subject of laysa.

positions.position: It is an active participle qualifying an omitted soul or person who lies.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī supply nafs; al-Samīn calls li-waqʿatihā the fronted predicate and kādhiba the delayed subject. Al-Ālūsī prefers nafs to an omitted maqāla because a person is more ordinarily called a liar than a statement; Ibn ʿĀshūr derives the form from intransitive kadhiba. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī compare the lām in 89:24.

positions.position: It qualifies an omitted state, case, report, or statement rather than a person.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī gives an omitted noun meaning no false case. Ibn ʿAṭiyya supplies an omitted ḥāl, with either a true report or an occurrence that cannot fail; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn report this circumstantial analysis. Al-Qurṭubī allows state or person, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī report or case. Al-Ālūsī considers maqāla less idiomatic than nafs.

positions.position: The feminine ending intensifies the expression.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī relates this possibility to his account of the ending in al-wāqiʿa.

positions.position: An active participle shape can carry a passive sense while keeping active participle agreement.
positions.reasons: Al-Fārisī says the passive meaning does not alter the pronoun's raising because the form follows the active participle pattern.

turns_on: Whether the form functions as a verbal noun, modifies an omitted person or state, intensifies the noun, or carries a passive sense in active form.

question: What does the verse say cannot occur at the Event?

positions.position: Nothing can repel, reverse, or recall the Event once it comes.
positions.reasons: Muqātil and Qatāda also deny a second occurrence or return; al-Māwardī reports Qatāda's addition that there is no consultation. Al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutayba cite Abū Tharwān's Banū Numayr idiom for absence of rebuttal; Ibn Qutayba adds that an attacker who does not 'lie' does not retreat. Al-Zajjāj compares an unretreating charge. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī cite the assault idiom and Zuhayr's lion line for not faltering. Ibn Kathīr cites 42:47, 70:1–2, and 6:73 for God's irresistible will. Al-Ālūsī presents this discouragement or holding-back sense but prefers the Event's certain truth.

positions.position: No one can deny the Event's occurrence when it becomes manifest.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kāmil explicitly includes believer and unbeliever. Al-Zamakhsharī contrasts present denial with affirmation then; al-Thaʿlabī reports Sībawayh's 'no denier.' Al-Rāzī gives both personal and verbal-noun construals. Al-Qāshānī says each witnesses his own happiness or misery. Elmalılı adds that no one escapes its impact. The Study Quran says it overwhelms former deniers. Al-Ālūsī also pictures a futile question addressed to the Hour as representational metaphor, imagined or literal.

positions.position: No soul will then lie about God or deny the unseen; all will acknowledge the truth.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī and Abū Ḥayyān cite professions of faith upon seeing punishment (40:84), delayed belief (26:201), and persistent doubt until the Hour (22:55). Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī compare 89:24. Bursawī specifies that claims of God's partners, child, or spouse and denial of raising the dead end then. Abū Ḥayyān criticizes al-Zamakhsharī's extensive treatment.

positions.position: Its occurrence and the report of it are true; no false case or falsehood belongs to it.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī and al-Kisāʾī say the Event contains no falsehood. Al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī compare the absence of idle speech in 88:11. Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes the report's truth from unfailing occurrence. Al-Ṭabrisī invokes transmitted evidence and reason. Al-Biqāʿī extends the certainty to every promised event arriving and every denied event staying absent. Bursawī offers a causal lām. Al-Ālūsī prefers this sense as clearer, while noting the rarity of fāʿila as a verbal noun.

positions.position: The Event's occurrence itself cannot fail; it must come to pass.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya illustrates a person who does not fail when carrying out a task; al-Samīn compares a promiser who does not lie. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb says the Event must happen. Ibn ʿĀshūr, citing Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, explains metaphorical 'lying' of a failed cause through Arabic attributions of speech to non-speaking things: Abū al-Najm's speaking girths and 'lying' garments.

positions.position: No self can falsely reassure its owner that the Event's terror is bearable.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī invokes the idiom of a soul emboldening someone before danger and compares people to scattered moths in 101:4. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Rāzī, and al-Ālūsī give the great-ordeal idiom; al-Kashf explains the lām as temporal. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the self-deception as transitive kadhdhaba and compares an eye deceiving its owner about what it saw. Abū Ḥayyān calls al-Zamakhsharī's elaboration excessive.

positions.position: The Day's terror prevents even a great liar from lying.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī calls this the intensive construal and explicitly prefers it for conveying the Day's horror.

positions.position: Anyone denying the Event then would be an immense liar.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī presents this as an alternative to the construal in which terror silences even a great liar, and says the latter better expresses the Day's horror.

positions.position: No one lies about anything at that time.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī says the overwhelming Event prevents lying generally. Al-Ālūsī says this depends on accepting that no one lies then and explaining the deniers' oath in 6:23.

positions.position: The Resurrection is wholly serious, without jest.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī reports this as another explanation.

turns_on: The senses of kādhiba range from retreat or failure, to denial by a person, to falsehood in reports or circumstances, to self-deception; the omitted noun and the lām affect which applies.

question: How does this clause function in the opening sentence?

positions.position: It supplies the answer to 'when the Event occurs' in verse 1.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı prefers this apparent construction. The Study Quran reads idhā and verse 2 continuously as an adverbial clause. Al-Zamakhsharī's reported alternative allows the clause as a conditional answer; Abū Ḥayyān rejects making laysa itself govern idhā because laysa has no event or time, citing the Friday example where the preposed predicate governs the temporal phrase.

positions.position: It is a parenthesis or interpolation between the condition and its response.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān adopts this analysis. Al-Samīn says it has no syntactic position and the answer is omitted. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, as reported by al-Ālūsī, also allows a parenthesis confirming the Event's certainty.

positions.position: It is a circumstantial clause describing the Event.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives it accusative circumstantial status. Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī makes al-wāqiʿa its circumstantial referent, governed by waqaʿat, giving three states of one referent; if all clauses are circumstantial, the governor of idhā is omitted, for example yuḥāsabūn. Abū Ḥayyān notes that grammarians dispute the number and classification of these circumstantial clauses and predicates.

positions.position: It stands as an independent opening sentence with no syntactic position.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī says this follows if idhā is governed by laysa, but not if the clause is the conditional answer or idhā is the object of an implied udhkur. Al-Samīn also allows an opening without syntactic position. Abū Ḥayyān rejects laysa governing a temporal adverb because laysa has no event or time.

turns_on: Whether verse 2 answers the opening idhā, interrupts a condition and its answer, describes the Event circumstantially, or opens independently; analyses differ on what governs idhā.

question: How is the following 'lowering, raising' phrase attached?

positions.position: It attaches to the earlier statement, not to the immediately later clause.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿUbayda says attachment to the later clause would require the accusative; Arabic may shift repeated predication from accusative to nominative, as in 70:15–17 and an anonymous rajaz line.

question: What does the Event reveal about people's states?

positions.position: It exposes pretence and distinguishes the safe and honored from those who meet regret and loss.
positions.reasons: Al-Qushayrī says soundness and uprightness lead to safety and honor, while deviation leads to regret and loss; he cites a poem in which tears on faces distinguish a true mourner from a pretender.

positions.position: Each person witnesses happiness or misery as the Event lowers the wretched and raises the fortunate.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī links that direct witnessing to the impossibility of denying the Event.

positions.position: It proves the deniers wrong and leaves them disgraced and foolish before the gathered.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr makes this a warning to those who deny Resurrection before it occurs.

turns_on: The notes draw distinct consequences: exposure of sincerity, witnessed felicity or misery, and disgrace for former deniers.
